final_task_tree.title: Figure out a training plan for my dog
final_task_tree.description:
Rescue border collie mix, 14 months. Pulls hard on the leash and barks at every other dog on walks. South Bay, California; I can do evenings and weekends.

Three things only:
1. Whether to hire a trainer or do it myself.
2. If hiring — two or three local options with real prices.
3. A week-by-week plan for the first four weeks.

Don't research anything beyond those three.

2. **3 South Bay options with real prices**: South Bay Dog Training group class in Campbell ($360/5wk, positive reinforcement, purpose-built for this exact "fine off-leash, reactive on-leash" pattern); D For Dogz private coaching ($2,400/6wk) or day training ($4,200/6wk), positive reinforcement, serves most of South Bay; Off Leash K9 Training San Jose ($500 first lesson + $100/session, e-collar-based — listed for comparison only, not the recommended fit).
3. **4-week plan** drafted week by week, covering equipment, loose-leash mechanics, and threshold-distance reactivity work, scheduled around evenings/weekends.

Full detail is in the attached report. One subtask remains open for you: pick a trainer option and make contact — all phone numbers/emails are in that subtask's description. Setting this to waiting since that's the only piece left.

report.markdown:
# Training Plan: 14-Month Rescue Border Collie Mix (Leash Pulling + Dog Reactivity)

## 1. Hire a trainer, or DIY?

**Recommendation: Hybrid.** DIY the leash pulling; get a trainer involved for the dog-reactive barking.

- **Leash pulling** is a mechanical skill most owners can teach solo with consistency: front-clip harness, stop-when-pulling, reward loose leash. No professional required for this piece alone.
- **Barking at every other dog on walks is "leash reactivity"** — a fear- or frustration-driven behavior, not defiance. <cite index="2-1,2-2">For other dogs, it might be best to get help from a professional dog trainer with leash reactivity experience, and your dog might also benefit from a consult with a veterinary behaviorist.</cite> Sources are clear it's very workable — <cite index="4-6,4-7">dog reactivity is a highly modifiable behavior, and through prevention, training and practice, even the most "explosive" dog can learn to show different behaviors and feel calmer in the presence of other dogs</cite> — but a rescue with unknown history at the high-arousal, adolescent 14-month mark is exactly the profile where a couple of professional sessions pays for itself: getting an accurate read on trigger distance and correct technique before habits get reinforced the wrong way.

**Suggested path:** book an initial private assessment (or a reactive-dog group class built for this exact profile), then run daily reps yourself between sessions using the week-by-week plan below.

## 2. Local South Bay Trainer Options (real prices)

| Trainer | Location/Area | Format | Price | Method | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **South Bay Dog Training** (Nathalie) | Campbell, CA | Group class, "Reactive Dog Level 1" | **$360 / 5 weeks** (4×45-min in-person + weekly Zoom Q&A + daily support group) | Force-free / positive reinforcement (Fear Free, PPG, IAABC, CCPDT affiliated) | Explicitly built for dogs fine off-leash with other dogs but reactive **on leash** — matches this dog's profile closely. Next session starts Aug 16, 2026 (Sun 11am), listed full; ask about the 12pm slot they mentioned adding. Contact: southbaydogtrainers@gmail.com |
| **D For Dogz** (Kaajal "KT" Tiwary) | San Jose, Santa Clara, Sunnyvale, Campbell, Los Gatos, Cupertino, Mountain View, Palo Alto, etc. | Private coaching or trainer-led "day training" | **Private Coaching: $2,400 / 6 weeks** (90-min initial consult + weekly sessions). **Day Training: $4,200 / 6 weeks** (trainer works dog directly twice/week, you join every 3rd session) | Positive reinforcement / force-free, Karen Pryor Academy certified | Free 15-minute phone consult before committing. Phone: 650-538-3011 |
| **Off Leash K9 Training of San Jose** | San Jose + surrounding South Bay | Private lessons | **$500 first lesson** (incl. e-collar + 20ft leash), **$100/session after**; 8-lesson reactivity package built on this | Balanced training, uses e-collar | Listed for price comparison only — e-collar/balanced methods are not the recommended starting approach for fear-based reactivity in a rescue with unknown history. Free phone consult offered. dogtrainerssanjose.com |

**Bottom line on cost:** the group class ($360) is by far the cheapest and is purpose-built for this exact "fine off-leash, reactive on-leash" pattern, but needs a second household to enroll and the near-term session is full. The private positive-reinforcement option (D For Dogz) costs considerably more ($2,400–$4,200) but guarantees 1:1 attention and flexible scheduling. The e-collar option is priced in between but uses a different training philosophy.

## 3. Week-by-Week Plan (First 4 Weeks)

Scheduled for evenings + weekends. Daily reps should be short (5–10 min), several times a day — better than one long session.

### Week 1 — Equipment & Foundations (no other-dog exposure yet)
- Buy a **front-clip harness** (e.g., Freedom No-Pull, Balance Harness) and a **6ft leash (no retractable)**. <cite index="50-12,50-13">If you attach the leash to the front of a harness on your dog's chest, you have control over your dog's center of gravity, and when the dog tries to pull forward, he is gently turned to face you.</cite>
- Call/email your chosen trainer to book the initial consult (see subtask for contacts).
- In the yard or driveway: practice name-recognition ("look at me") and the stop-and-go loose-leash method — <cite index="55-1,55-2">when the dog pulls on the lead, bring it back to your side and loosen the lead, and repeat every time the dog does this.</cite>
- No walks near other dogs this week — keep exposure controlled while the mechanics are being built.

### Week 2 — Loose Leash on the Road + Reactivity Threshold
- Take the stop-and-go loose-leash drill onto real sidewalks in low-distraction areas (quiet streets, early morning/late evening).
- Start reactivity work: find the **distance at which your dog first notices another dog but does not yet bark/lunge** (their "threshold"). Stay at or beyond that distance only.
- At threshold distance, practice "engage-disengage" or "look at that": <cite index="5-4,5-5">observation games like engage-disengage and look at that use counter conditioning principles to help your dog feel calmer around their triggers, then capitalize on operant conditioning to create better responses like looking at you rather than barking and lunging.</cite>
- If your dog does react, don't punish — quietly increase distance (a U-turn or step off the path) and reset.

### Week 3 — Close the Distance, Keep Building Loose Leash
- Gradually and only as your dog succeeds, decrease the trigger distance in small increments. <cite index="8-3,8-4">Work with your trainer to practice these skills in the presence of a calm dog outside of the range in which your dog is fixated on them, then weekly reduce the distance of the other dog until you are as close as you need to be for a walk.</cite>
- Layer in real walk routes at quieter times of day so both skills (loose leash + calm-around-dogs) are practiced together, not in isolation.
- Keep rewarding loose leash throughout every walk, not just during dedicated reactivity reps — consistency is what locks in the habit.

### Week 4 — Combine & Review
- Run a normal neighborhood walk combining loose-leash walking and threshold work for reactivity.
- If you know a calm, dog-friendly neighbor's dog, arrange a brief controlled pass at a safe distance (not a greeting) to test progress.
- Check in with your trainer (or attend the second in-person session if in a group class) to review progress and set goals for weeks 5–8. Reactivity work is a longer arc — <cite index="5-9,5-10,5-11,5-12">successfully working with a reactive dog requires a long-term commitment, and finding the right approach may involve trying different methods and adjusting strategies; focus on gradual progress and celebrate small improvements.</cite>

## What's Left For You
- Decide which trainer option fits your budget and pick up the phone/email (see the "Contact chosen trainer" subtask for exact contact info).
- Everything else — equipment, the 4-week structure, and the reasoning behind hiring vs. DIY — is above and ready to act on immediately.

subtasks.title: Decide: hire a trainer vs. DIY for leash pulling + dog-reactive barking
subtasks.description:
RECOMMENDATION: Hybrid — hire a trainer for the reactivity piece, DIY the leash-pulling piece.

Reasoning:
- Loose-leash walking (pulling) is a well-documented, mechanical skill most owners can teach themselves with consistent daily practice (stop-and-go, direction changes, positive reinforcement, a front-clip harness). No professional needed for this alone.
- Barking/lunging at other dogs is leash reactivity, a fear- or frustration-driven behavior. Sources agree it's manageable, but recommend professional help when: the dog is intensely aroused, you can't read the triggers, or the behavior is escalating/embarrassing/stressful for you. AKC notes some dogs can be worked through with owner-only techniques, but others do best with a professional trainer experienced in leash reactivity, and a vet behaviorist consult can help if the dog is too aroused to learn.
- Rescue + adolescent (14mo) border collie mix = unknown bite/trigger history and a breed prone to high arousal and fixation, both of which make a couple of professional sessions worth the cost — mainly to get an accurate read on the trigger distance/threshold and correct technique before habits (yours or the dog's) get reinforced the wrong way.

Recommended path: Book an initial private assessment + 3-4 follow-up private sessions (not a group class yet — dog is not ready to be near other dogs at group-class distance) with a force-free/positive-reinforcement trainer who explicitly lists leash reactivity experience. Use the trainer's session to set the plan, then run the daily reps yourself between sessions (evenings/weekends). See sibling task for 2-3 local South Bay options with prices.

subtasks.title: Draft week-by-week training plan for first 4 weeks
subtasks.description:
Four-week plan drafted covering both leash pulling and dog-reactive barking, scheduled for evenings/weekends. Full week-by-week detail is in the parent task's report. Summary:
- Week 1: Equipment + foundations. Get a front-clip harness (e.g. Freedom No-Pull, Balance Harness) and 6ft leash (no retractable). Book trainer consult. Practice name-recognition/"look at me" and loose-leash stop-and-go in the yard/driveway (no other-dog exposure needed yet).
- Week 2: Take loose-leash mechanics on the road in low-distraction areas; begin reactivity threshold work — identify the distance at which the dog first notices another dog without reacting ("under threshold") and practice engage-disengage/"look at that" at that distance only.
- Week 3: Gradually decrease trigger distance as the dog succeeds; add real walk routes at quieter times; keep reinforcing loose leash throughout, not just during reactivity reps.
- Week 4: Combine loose-leash + reactivity skills on a normal neighborhood walk; introduce brief passes with one known calm dog at a safe distance if available; review progress with trainer and set weeks 5-8 goals.
